title: He's Just Not That Into You
full_review:
A gaggle of Baltimore yuppies is schooled in the rules allegedly governing modern-day romance in the glossy ensemble comedy-drama "He's Just Not That Into You" (Warner Bros.).

Based on a book penned by two writers who contributed to the HBO series "Sex and the City," the material is not especially incisive or entertaining. And although not terribly cynical or raunchy, the characters often act in morally dubious ways as they're disabused of multiple preconceptions vis-a-vis dating and marriage.

The film looks good, but its awkward structure and stilted pacing suggest that one season of a cable TV series has been compressed and, to an insufficient degree, sanitized for the multiplex.

Because the performances are solid, its primary appeal will be as a showcase for a clutch of established and up-and-coming actors. While he bathes his handsome cast in a pleasing golden light, director Ken Kwapis is unable to generate appreciable amounts of flattering humor, drama or insight.

The main story lines are traceable to three female colleagues who, occupying adjacent cubicles, dish about their love lives. Gigi (Ginnifer Goodwin) is a single twentysomething with a sweet disposition and an idealistic outlook. She's frustrated by all the men she meets or dates who say they are going to call but never do. Alex (Justin Long), a womanizing bar manager, takes her under his wing and offers harsh truths about male attitudes toward relationships.

Beth (Jennifer Anniston) has lived with her boyfriend, Neil (Ben Affleck), for seven years and desperately wants to get married. Aware of Neil's feelings on the subject, she has never insisted on a proposal until now, the eve of her sister's nuptials.

Janine (Jennifer Connelly) and her husband, Ben (Bradley Cooper), are in the midst of renovating a row house when he meets an attractive young woman in the supermarket checkout line. Equally smitten, Anna (Scarlett Johansson) pursues Ben, aware of his marital status yet unbothered by her home-wrecking aspirations. Meanwhile, she strings along her sometime boyfriend, Conor (Kevin Connolly).

On the periphery of this circle is Anna's friend, Mary (Drew Barrymore), who sells advertising for a gay newspaper. Encouraged by her male workmates, she's stuck in cyberspace when it comes to romance, only able to meet and communicate with eligible men on the Internet and via electronic devices.

Upbeat resolutions partially offset the film's problematic sexual content and times when the characters act in ways contrary to their better natures. Traditional values and the institution of marriage are affirmed eventually. The advice doled out sends a contradictory message, however. On the one hand, we're told that meaningful relationships require strenuous effort to establish and maintain. On the other, we're left with the impression that it's better not to try too hard.

The film contains frequent sexual references, some nonexplicit sexual encounters, including the adulterous and out-of-wedlock variety, a story line centered on cohabitation, frequent crude language, an instance of rough language, and a few scatological references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
